title: Morning glory
hookLine: Chiyo-ni finds a morning glory wrapped round the well bucket and borrows water elsewhere
tomorrow: moonlight on the floor, like frost. what does the poet think of?

lines: A VINE AROUND THE BUCKET ROPE.
cards: Mornings run on rails: kettle, tap, cup, no thought at all. One morning the poet Chiyo-ni goes out to the well and the rails stop.
Overnight a morning glory has wound its vine around the bucket rope, and its flowers are open. To draw water, she'd have to tear it. So she doesn't.
She takes her bucket next door and asks for some. Her poem: asagao ni, tsurube torarete, morai mizu. The morning glory has taken the well bucket: borrowed water.

teach.h: THE ROPE, THE FLOWERS, THE WALK.
teach.b: Feel the scene. The cold, wet rope. The blue of the flowers.
The weight of an empty bucket on the walk to a neighbor's door, and a full one on the way back.

teach.h: THE WEIGHT IS ON THE BORROWING.
teach.b: Notice where the poem puts its weight: not on the flower, on the borrowing. Chiyo-ni pays for the vine with her own trouble.
Tradition says she later took vows as a Buddhist nun, and her poem lines up with a quiet rule in the Vinaya, the code for Buddhist monks and nuns: they are not to cut or destroy growing plants.

Buddhist teaching asks for a light step through the living world, and here that step costs one short walk. There's one more thing to feel. A morning glory opens in the morning and closes by afternoon.
Chiyo-ni wasn't giving up her well forever.

teach.h: LET A SHORT LIFE FINISH ITS DAY.
teach.b: She was letting a short life finish its one day. So the teaching under the poem is this: in Buddhism, not harming reaches even the green things, and sometimes the kind way is to go around.
One detail worth passing on: the last two words, morai mizu, mean water you received, a small gift you had to ask for.

how: Buddhist monks and nuns keep a Vinaya rule against destroying growing plants. Haiku readers know Chiyo-ni's morning glory poem as a picture of gentleness that costs the poet a little trouble.

o: a vine flower that opens at dawn and shuts by afternoon
the temple bell that monks ring at the break of day
a Japanese summer festival for greeting the sunrise

games.q: the well, the vine, the rule: tap the pairs.
p: the well bucket on its rope
the code for Buddhist monks and nuns

s: Chiyo-ni's poem is mostly about how pretty the flower is
the weight falls on the last words: borrowed water. she pays for the vine with her own trouble.
the Buddhist monastic code forbids destroying growing plants
it's in the Vinaya, the rule for monks and nuns.
Chiyo-ni tore the vine, then felt bad about it
she left it and went next door for water.

games.q: a vine has grown over the bike rack at work, flowers open. you need your bike. what fits Chiyo-ni's poem?
o: park by the fence for now; the flowers won't last long.
cut it; plants don't feel anything, so it doesn't matter.
never use the rack again; touching plants is wrong.
games.why: Chiyo-ni didn't tear the vine, and didn't make a law of it either. she borrowed water for a morning.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or picture one. Hold it and feel its weight, then take one slow sip and taste it, cold or plain. This water came from somewhere, the way Chiyo-ni's came from next door.
Set the glass down, and leave everything near you undisturbed while you sit.

wordCard.voice: Morning glory: a vine that opens for one morning, and Chiyo-ni's reason to borrow water rather than tear it.

carryVoice: For the road: borrowed water, so a short life can finish its day. That's the last haiku stop.
